content: Participants in the control group were permitted to maintain their usual intake of free sugars or reduce their consumption of free sugars. This definition is specific to randomized trials assessing body weight outcomes. Although some statistical heterogeneity was observed, the studies consistently demonstrated a positive association between increased free sugar intake and weight gain. Short-term studies were of sufficient duration to detect changes in the outcomes of interest, providing relevant evidence for the relationship between higher free sugar consumption and weight gain. However, the funnel plot suggested potential publication bias, leading to a downgrading of the evidence. Eight cohort studies contributed to the evaluation of the impact of sugar intake on dental caries. There was no evidence of bias risk, and six of the eight studies accounted for fluoride exposure. A consistent association between free sugar intake and dental caries was identified. No evidence of inconsistency was found, and seven of the eight studies reported higher levels of dental caries with increased sugar consumption. Due to the unsuitability of the data for pooling, formal heterogeneity assessment was not possible. Evidence was not downgraded for indirectness for several reasons. All eight cohort studies were conducted in children, but the etiology of dental caries is similar in children and adults, despite the softer and more vulnerable enamel in primary dentition. Although no cohort studies were conducted in adults, data from five other study designs in adults included in the systematic review showed a statistically significant positive relationship between dietary free sugars and dental caries levels. The negative health effects of dental caries are cumulative, persisting from childhood (permanent dentition) into adulthood. Four of the eight cohort studies included permanent dentition. Studies were conducted across diverse populations worldwide, including Argentina, Brazil, England, Finland, South Africa, Sweden, and the United States. Six of the eight cohort studies directly reported on free sugar consumption or its components, such as added sugars. Rugg-Gunn et al. initially reported total sugar intake but later assessed the percentage of added sugars in their original cohort study, confirming a positive correlation between total sugar and added sugar intake. Burt et al. intended to measure various sugars but were unable to do so due to the unavailability of relevant food composition data at the time. Based on the findings of Rugg-Gunn et al., it was assumed that a similar relationship between total sugar and added sugar intake would apply to the Burt et al. cohort study, which was therefore retained in the analysis. Data from the eight cohort studies were not suitable for pooling, but evidence of a large effect was observed in some individual studies. For example, Rodrigues et al. and Rugg-Gunn et al. reported significant effects over two years, with each 100 g/day increase in free sugar intake associated with higher caries levels. Ruottinen et al. also reported significant findings for the low-sugar group. However, the study by Battelino et al. suggested a large effect, likely overestimated due to confounding by socioeconomic status. Other studies did not report effect sizes for caries. The dose-response effect noted in the Rugg-Gunn et al. cohort study was supported by ecological studies, and the evidence was upgraded once for the large effect size. The total number of participants from the eight cohort studies was substantial. Standard indices such as DMFS (decayed, missing, or filled dental surfaces), DMFT (decayed, missing, or filled teeth), and dmft/DMFT (decayed, missing, or filled primary dentition and/or teeth) were used to measure outcomes. Confidence intervals (CI), odds ratios (OR), and standard deviations (SD) were also reported. In studies assessing the effect of reducing free sugar intake in children, participants in the intervention group reduced their free sugar consumption compared to the control group, which maintained their usual intake. This definition applied specifically to randomized trials evaluating body mass index (BMI). Five cohort studies reported data on the odds of being overweight at follow-up in children consuming approximately one daily serving of sugar-sweetened beverages at baseline compared to those consuming none or very little. Data from 14 other cohort studies with 33 comparisons were used to test a dose-response effect, but the results were inconclusive. Five cohort studies contributed to the assessment of the effect of reducing sugar intake to below 10% of total energy intake on dental caries. There was no evidence of bias risk, and all studies accounted for fluoride exposure. A consistent association between free sugar intake and caries was detected. No evidence of inconsistency was found, and all five studies reported higher levels of dental caries with higher sugar intake when comparing free sugar intake above 10% of total energy to below 10%.
